text.p: This is how major world bond markets were trading in late European business on Tuesday.

GERMANY - Bund futures were convincingly higher again in late trading but off earlier highs as U.S. Treasuries weighed on sentiment. The June Bund future on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) was trading at 101.84, up 0.09.

BRITAIN - British gilt futures ended easier and well below opening levels as the initial impetus provided by a supportive retail sales survey was eroded by the softer tone on international markets, especially in the U.S. The June long gilt future on LIFFE was trading at 111-25/32, down 03/32 from Monday's settlement price.

FRANCE - French bond futures posted a small gain after a session driven largely by intra-day traders who bought in the morning and sold before the close as U.S. bonds declined. The March notional bond future on the MATIF in Paris settled at 131.20 up 0.08 from Monday's settlement price.

ITALY - Italian debt markets gave up a firmer start and followed U.S. Treasuries and the bund market lower by later afternoon while the lira's early strength soon ran out of steam, dealers said. The June bond future on LIFFE was trading at 126.68 down 0.52 from Monday's settlement price.

UNITED STATES - U.S. Treasuries were stuck near their New York closing levels by midday, as investors were cautious before the release of the Beige Book on Wednesday and a series of economic indicators this week. The June Treasury bond future on the Chicago Board of Trade was trading at 109-22/32, down 14/32 from Monday's settlement price. The long bond was quoted to yield 6.86 percent.
JAPAN - The key June JGB contract ended higher in Tokyo, ignoring the release of strong economic data in the afternoon, while the cash JGB yield fell to a record low of 2.320 percent.

EUROBONDS - The main focus for the primary market on Tuesday was Belgium's $500 million five year Euro-Asian bond, launched earlier in Japan. The deal was priced to yield nine basis points over U.S. Treasury notes. An official at joint lead manager Morgan Stanley said the issue had gone extremely well, with strong demand from non-Japan Asia and Swiss and Benelux investors in particular. "The pricing is very fair and this is the first sovereign benchmark for some time," the official said. UBS was the other joint lead manager.
